script.opening: “Hello doctor, it’s Idris’s mum. I sent a photo of his lip this morning — have you had a chance to look at it? I don’t know what it is.”

facts.text: “It came up on Monday — so two days. Little blisters on the bottom lip, on one side. They really hurt him and they itch.”
“Now you say it — the day before, he kept saying his lip was tingly and burning.”
“He had a horrible cold last week — runny nose, sore throat, temperature for a couple of days. He’s over that now.”

facts.topic: Inside the mouth, eating and drinking (if asked)
facts.text: “No ulcers in his mouth or on his gums that I can see. He’s eating his dinner fine and drinking normally. Weeing normally.”
“No, his eyes are fine — not red, not sore, no problems with the light.”
“Nothing anywhere else. His eczema is behind his knees and on his hands but it’s calm at the moment — no new spots or blisters there.”
“He’s fine in himself — running about, no temperature now. I’ve given him Calpol twice and it helped.”

facts.topic: What you have put on it (only if asked about treatment)
facts.text: “I’ve been dabbing some of his eczema cream on it — the hydrocortisone. I thought it might calm it down.”
“Never had anything like this. I don’t know anyone with blisters.” If asked about relatives: “My dad gets those sore lips sometimes — he was round last week for the baby.”
“Me, my husband Faisal, Idris and the baby, Amira — she’s three weeks old. I’m breastfeeding.” If asked about contact: “Idris is obsessed with her — he kisses her head all the time.”
No sores on your breasts or nipples; feeding is going well.
“I kept him off yesterday and today. Can he go back?”

Be friendly but tired (new baby). You are mainly worried it is “something infectious”. Mention the baby only when asked who is at home or who he has contact with. If the doctor says “herpes”, sound shocked: “Herpes? Isn’t that something people catch from sex? How has my son got that?” — and quietly add “I don’t want people thinking things about our family.” Settle if this is explained kindly and simply. If the baby risk is explained, become anxious: “Has he already given it to her?” Accept the advice offered.

ice.ideas: “Maybe an allergy, or impetigo — the school had a letter about impetigo.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the new baby: she has not thought about the risk to a 3-week-old, and Idris kisses her constantly. Once the word “herpes” is used she worries it is sexually transmitted and that relatives or the school will judge the family.
ice.expectations: To be told what it is, whether it is catching, what to put on it, and when he can go back to school.

cues: “I don’t know what it is.” — wants a clear name and explanation.
“He’s obsessed with the baby.” — the contact risk to a 3-week-old.
“I don’t want people thinking things.” — stigma attached to the word “herpes”.

checkpoints.text: Clarifies the history and the photograph: onset, prodromal tingling, pain, blisters and crusting, recent cold, first episode, and treatment used (finds the hydrocortisone on the sore)

Screens for complications: mouth and gum ulcers or drooling (gingivostomatitis), eye pain, redness or photophobia, spread into eczema areas with fever (eczema herpeticum), fever, fluid intake and urine output
Asks who lives at home and finds the 3-week-old breastfed sister and the close contact; reaches a diagnosis of herpes labialis (cold sore)

Explains a self-limiting cold sore (about 7–10 days); stops the steroid on the sore; paracetamol or ibuprofen; optional over-the-counter aciclovir 5% cream with honest benefit; no need for antibiotics or oral antivirals; no school exclusion

Gives specific newborn protection: no kissing or face-to-face contact with the baby, hand washing before handling her, no shared towels or cups, until the sore has fully healed; breastfeeding can continue

Safety-nets clearly for both children: baby with any blisters, fever, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness or floppiness — urgent same-day assessment or 999; Idris with spreading painful sores in eczema areas, fever, eye symptoms or not drinking — same-day review
Explains HSV-1 without stigma (usually caught in childhood from a kiss or shared cup, not sexual), responds to the worry about being judged, and avoids blaming the grandfather or the mother
Responds calmly to “Has he already given it to her?”, checks understanding with teach-back and agrees what to do next

worked.lbl: Use the photo, then the history
worked.txt: “Thank you for the photo — it’s really helpful. Before I tell you what I think, can I ask a few questions? Did he feel anything on his lip before the blisters came up?”
“Who else is at home with Idris? … And how close is he with the baby — does he cuddle or kiss her?”

“This is a cold sore. It’s caused by a very common virus — the same family as herpes, which I know sounds alarming — but this type is usually caught in childhood from a kiss from a relative or a shared cup. It’s nothing to do with sex, and around half of adults carry it.”

“The one thing I want to be really careful about is Amira. Very young babies can get seriously unwell from this virus. So, until the sore has completely healed, no kisses for her from Idris, and everyone washes hands before picking her up. You can carry on breastfeeding.”

“Please stop the eczema cream on the sore — steroid creams can make a virus spread. Calpol or ibuprofen for the pain. A pharmacy cream called aciclovir can shorten it slightly, but it works best at the tingly stage, so it’s one to keep for next time.”

“He can go back to school tomorrow — just no sharing drinks. If Amira has any spots or blisters, a temperature, isn’t feeding or is floppy or very sleepy, ring 999 or go to A&E straight away. If Idris’s sores spread to his eczema, he gets a fever or a sore red eye, call us the same day.”

f.learning: Herpes labialis is common and self-limiting, but the GP task is to look around the lesion — at the child’s eczema, eyes and hydration, and at who else is in the house. Recurrent HSV-1 typically follows a prodrome of tingling and may be triggered by a cold, fever, sunlight or stress; lesions crust and heal in about 7–10 days. Topical aciclovir offers only a modest benefit if started early, so it is optional; oral antivirals are reserved for primary gingivostomatitis needing treatment, severe or frequent recurrences or immunocompromise. Steroid creams should not be applied to the lesion. The safety issues are eczema herpeticum (a dermatological emergency — rapidly spreading, painful punched-out erosions in eczematous skin, often with fever) and herpes in a newborn, which can be disseminated or affect the brain; the infant may look only mildly unwell at first, so any vesicles, fever, poor feeding or lethargy in a baby under 3 months needs emergency assessment. Children with cold sores do not need to be kept off school. Language matters: explaining that HSV-1 is usually acquired in childhood by non-sexual contact removes stigma and makes the infection-control advice more likely to be followed.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CKS — Herpes simplex, oral (accessed October 2026) · UKHSA — Health protection in children and young people settings, including education (2022) · NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management (2019)
knowledge.summary: Cold sore in a well child: reassure, stop the steroid on the lesion, analgesia, optional OTC aciclovir — and protect the 3-week-old baby, with clear red flags for neonatal herpes and eczema herpeticum.

points.t: Prodromal tingling or burning for hours to a day, then grouped vesicles on a red base at the lip border, crusting over several days, healing in about 7–10 days without scarring. Common triggers: intercurrent illness or fever, sunlight, stress, local trauma.

Self-care: paracetamol or ibuprofen, avoid picking, petroleum jelly for cracking. Topical aciclovir 5% cream (pharmacy) five times daily for 5 days may shorten an episode slightly if started in the prodrome; benefit is small once blisters are established. Usual dose for a child of this age: as the adult cream regimen (NICE CKS/SPC; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: aciclovir 5% cream). Do not apply corticosteroids to the lesion.

Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis with significant pain or poor intake (within the first few days), immunocompromise, frequent or severe recurrences — on clinical judgement; seek specialist advice for neonates and the immunocompromised.

Clusters of painful vesicles or monomorphic punched-out erosions spreading rapidly in eczematous skin, often with fever and malaise. Needs same-day treatment with oral or intravenous aciclovir; refer immediately if around the eyes or the child is unwell.

Neonatal HSV can be disseminated or cause encephalitis with high mortality, and early signs may be subtle. Anyone with an active cold sore should not kiss a baby, should wash hands before contact, and should not share towels or cups. Breastfeeding continues unless there are lesions on the breast. A baby under 3 months with fever of 38 °C or above is high risk (NICE NG143).
UKHSA guidance: no exclusion is needed for cold sores; avoid kissing and sharing cups, and encourage hand hygiene.

The Clear pass candidate finds the newborn in the house, gives practical protection without frightening the mother, removes the stigma from “herpes”, and safety-nets for both children in specific terms.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Rahman? I’m Dr Okafor, one of the GPs. Can I just check I’m speaking to Idris’s mum, and is he with you?
model.why: Confirms identity and relationship on a third-party call

model.text: Yes, I’m his mum. He’s in the garden. Did you see the photo? I don’t know what it is.
I did — thank you, it really helps. Tell me how it started.
model.why: Open question after acknowledging the photo

model.text: Two days ago, little blisters on his bottom lip. They hurt and itch.
Did he feel anything on the lip before they came up? And has he been unwell recently?
He said it was tingly the day before. And he had a bad cold last week with a temperature.
Any ulcers inside his mouth or on his gums, any trouble eating or drinking? Is he weeing normally? Any sore, red eyes?
No, he’s eating and drinking fine. Eyes are fine.
And his eczema — any new spots, blisters or sore patches there? Any fever now? Have you put anything on the lip?
model.why: Eczema herpeticum screen and treatment history

model.text: Eczema’s calm. No fever. I’ve been putting his hydrocortisone on it.
Thanks. Who else lives with you — and is there anyone very young or unwell at home?
My husband, and the baby — Amira, she’s three weeks. Idris kisses her all the time.
That’s really important, thank you. From the photo and what you’ve told me, this is a cold sore. It’s caused by a virus called herpes simplex type 1.
Herpes? Isn’t that from sex? How has my son got that? I don’t want people thinking things.

I can see why the word is worrying. This type is mainly caught in childhood — a kiss from a relative or sharing a cup — and about half of adults carry it. It’s nothing to do with sex, and nobody has done anything wrong. The cold last week probably woke it up.

It should crust and heal in about a week. Please stop the eczema cream on the sore — steroids can help a virus spread. Calpol or ibuprofen for pain. The pharmacy sells aciclovir cream; it helps only a little now, but is worth having ready for the tingle next time.
model.why: Treatment with honest benefit; stops the steroid

model.text: The main thing is Amira. Tiny babies can get very ill from this virus. Until the sore has completely healed: no kissing her, wash hands before anyone holds her, no sharing towels. You can carry on breastfeeding.
Has he already given it to her?

Most babies who are near a cold sore don’t catch it, so let’s not assume that. But watch her closely. If she has any blisters or spots, a temperature of 38 or more, isn’t feeding, or is floppy or unusually sleepy, call 999 or go straight to A&E — don’t wait.
model.why: Proportionate reassurance with an explicit emergency safety-net

model.text: For Idris: if sores spread over his eczema, he gets a fever or a red, sore eye, call us that day. He can go back to school tomorrow. Can you tell me the main things you’ll do?
model.why: Safety-net for the child and teach-back

model.text: No kissing Amira, wash hands, stop the steroid cream, and 999 if she’s got spots or a temperature or won’t feed.

social.t: A tired parent in the first weeks after birth may not think about infection risks; practical, specific instructions (hands, no kisses, separate towels) work better than general advice.
The word “herpes” carries sexual stigma. Explaining childhood, non-sexual transmission protects family relationships (the grandfather) and the child at school.

legal.t: Images of children sent through online consultation are part of the record: store them in the notes, share only for care, and record the parent’s consent.

professional.t: A good-quality photograph plus a targeted history is usually enough for a typical cold sore. Arrange a face-to-face review if the image is unclear, the child is unwell, or lesions are near the eye.
With consent, letting the health visitor know about the exposure is reasonable, as she is reviewing the baby.

community.t: Community pharmacists can advise on cold-sore creams and pain relief for children and know when to send a child back to the GP.

redFlags: Mouth and gum ulcers, drooling, not drinking (primary gingivostomatitis, dehydration)
Eye pain, redness, photophobia or lesions near the eye
Rapid spread in eczema areas with fever (eczema herpeticum)
Newborn or immunocompromised contact at home
psychosocial: Who lives at home — 3-week-old breastfed sister
Fear of judgement from family and school
ice: Concern: infectious; then stigma; then the baby

playbook.diagnosis: Herpes labialis (recurrent HSV-1 cold sore), first recognised episode, in a well child with quiescent eczema; newborn sibling at risk of exposure.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s a cold sore — a very common virus most people catch as children. It will heal on its own in about a week. The important thing is keeping it away from the baby.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried it was something catching, and then the word herpes worried you more. It is catching through close contact, but it’s a childhood virus — and with a few precautions we can protect Amira.”
management.psychosocial: Practical steps that fit a busy home with a newborn; reassurance that no one is to blame.
sharedPlan: Optional pharmacy aciclovir 5% cream; keep for the tingling stage next time
No kissing or face-to-face contact with the baby; hand washing; no shared towels or cups until fully healed
safetyNet: Baby: blisters, fever 38 °C or more, poor feeding, floppiness or unusual sleepiness — 999 or A&E
Idris: spreading sores on eczema, fever, eye pain or redness, not drinking — same-day GP or NHS 111
Not healed in 2 weeks — call back

pitfalls.intro: The diagnosis is easy. The station is failed by candidates who stop at the lip.

items.fail: Diagnoses a cold sore from the photo and never asks who lives at home.
items.why: The 3-week-old sister is the person at real risk; neonatal herpes can be fatal.
items.fix: Always ask about household contacts — especially babies, pregnancy and immunocompromise — for any infectious rash.

items.fail: Says the hydrocortisone “won’t hurt” or prescribes oral aciclovir or antibiotics routinely.
items.why: Steroids on a viral lesion can worsen it; oral antivirals and antibiotics are not needed for an uncomplicated cold sore in a well child.
items.fix: Stop the steroid, simple analgesia, optional OTC aciclovir with honest benefit.

items.fail: Answers “Isn’t herpes sexual?” with a technical lecture on HSV-1 and HSV-2, or ignores the comment about people judging the family.
items.why: The stigma is what the mother will carry away; leaving it unaddressed damages trust and family relationships.
items.fix: Simple words: caught in childhood from a kiss or a cup, very common, nobody’s fault.

Prodrome, trigger, mouth, eyes, eczema, hydration, treatment used — then the household and the baby.
Name the cold sore; remove the stigma; respond to the worry about judgement.
Stop steroid, analgesia, optional aciclovir cream, newborn protection, school.
Red flags for the baby and for Idris; teach-back.

wordPics.clearFail: Misses the newborn entirely, endorses the steroid cream or prescribes antibiotics, keeps the child off school unnecessarily, and gives no safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Correct diagnosis and treatment advice but never asks about the household, or mentions “avoid babies” in passing without specific actions or red flags; stigma question brushed off.
wordPics.pass: Focused history including eyes, mouth and eczema; diagnoses a cold sore; stops the steroid; finds the baby and gives clear hygiene advice with red flags; school advice correct.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, delivered warmly and efficiently: removes the stigma in one or two sentences, answers “Has he given it to her?” honestly and calmly, separate specific safety-nets for each child, and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s just a cold sore, nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “It’s a cold sore, which usually heals in a week — the main thing is keeping it away from the baby.”
avoid.why: Reassurance that ignores the newborn is unsafe.

avoid.dont: “Herpes is a sexually transmitted virus but this is type 1…”
avoid.instead: “This type is usually caught as a child, from a kiss or a shared cup — it’s nothing to do with sex.”
avoid.why: Plain language; removes rather than adds stigma.

avoid.dont: “Keep him off school until it’s gone.”
avoid.instead: “He can go back — just no sharing drinks, and wash hands.”
avoid.why: UKHSA advises no exclusion for cold sores.
